implementation_notes: Go's premature optimisation has two characteristic forms. The first is guessing at buffer and pool sizes — `make([]byte, 4096)` where the packet size is unknown, or a `sync.Pool` added 'for performance' before any allocation profile. The second, and more specific to Go, is concurrency: adding goroutines, channels and worker pools because the language makes them cheap, before any measurement shows the workload is concurrent at all, which produces ordering bugs and shutdown problems for no measured gain. The second is the Go form of the general rule and is exactly the failure the Go proverb warns about. The tooling is excellent: `go test -bench`, `pprof`, and `-race` as the minimum bar for any concurrency change.
idiom_name: buffer sizes and pool sizes guessed; hand-rolled pool before a profile
pitfalls: Worker pools and `sync.Pool` added without an allocation or CPU profile.
Channel buffer sizes guessed, which changes both latency and blocking behaviour without a stated requirement.
`select` with `default` turning a blocking design into a spin loop — a performance change that is also a correctness change.
Micro-optimising a hot loop when the real cost is the round trip to a dependency.
